questions.question: An adult with repaired tetralogy of Fallot without pulmonary atresia is now NYHA class II, with moderate pulmonary regurgitation. Four months ago the patient required hospitalization for heart failure. Which 2025 ACHD anatomic-physiological classification applies?
options: II-C
II-D
III-C
III-D
questions.explanation:
Anatomical Complexity and Physiological Stage

Correct answer: II-D

Two Independent Axes

**Anatomy: I simple, II moderate complexity, III great complexity.**

TOF without pulmonary atresia is II; TOF with pulmonary atresia is III.

**Physiology: A–D; use the highest applicable stage.**

Repair does not automatically make anatomy simple or physiology normal.

Apply the 2025 Time Window

**Heart-failure admission within 12 months establishes stage D.**

This admission was 4 months ago: II-D despite current NYHA II.

Current moderate PR alone would be a C feature; clinical improvement does not erase the recent D event.

**Reassess physiology over time to guide surveillance and procedural planning.**

Record the qualifying findings; symptoms, EF or anatomical labels alone are incomplete.

Stage | 2025 physiological criteria

A | Asymptomatic; no anatomical/hemodynamic sequelae or sustained arrhythmia; normal exercise capacity and pulmonary pressure.

B | Mild ventricular enlargement/dysfunction or native valve disease; normally functioning prosthetic valve; insignificant shunt; stable arrhythmia without treatment change for 12 months; pacemaker/ICD without ICD therapy for 12 months.

C | BNP/NT-proBNP ≥2× upper normal limit; significant shunt; resting saturation ==86–92%==; at least moderate valve disease or ventricular dysfunction; low-risk PAH; sustained/high-burden tachyarrhythmia needing drugs, ablation, cardioversion or ICD therapy within 12 months.

D | Heart-failure admission or endocarditis within 12 months; Eisenmenger syndrome; NYHA III/IV; recurrent hemodynamically important/refractory arrhythmia; resting saturation ==≤85%==; intermediate/high-risk PAH.

II-C: Anatomical II is correct; moderate PR is a C feature, but the recent heart-failure admission establishes the higher stage D.

III-C: Ordinary repaired TOF is anatomical II, not III; this option also overlooks the stage-D admission within 12 months.

III-D: Stage D is correct, but heart failure changes physiology rather than anatomical category; TOF without pulmonary atresia remains II.

ACC/AHA multisociety ACHD guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.09.006

questions.topic: Flow, oxygen transport and resistance calculations
questions.question: During stable catheterization on room air, systemic arterial saturation is 98%, pulmonary venous saturation 98%, representative pre-shunt mixed venous saturation 68% and pulmonary arterial saturation 83%. Assuming equal hemoglobin and negligible dissolved oxygen, what is Qp/Qs?
questions.explanation:
Pulmonary-to-Systemic Flow Ratio

Correct answer: 2.0

Calculation

**Fick shunt ratio:** Qp/Qs = (systemic arterial − mixed venous O₂ content)/(pulmonary venous − pulmonary arterial O₂ content).

**Substitution:** (98 − 68)/(98 − 83) = 30/15 = **2.0**. Pulmonary flow is twice systemic flow.

Interpretation and Limitations

**Saturation substitution** assumes comparable hemoglobin and negligible dissolved oxygen; high inspired oxygen can invalidate this shortcut.

**Sampling** requires steady physiology and representative mixed venous blood; incomplete mixing or anomalous venous return can distort the result.

**Closure assessment** combines shunt size, chamber enlargement, anatomy and PVR. Qp/Qs ≥1.5 supports significance but does not independently establish operability.

JACC Interventions: catheterization in adults with congenital heart disease, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcin.2021.12.020

questions.question: Which pairing correctly describes the dominant chamber volume-loading pattern of an uncomplicated significant left-to-right shunt before advanced pulmonary vascular disease develops?
options: ASD: right atrium and RV; VSD: left atrium and LV
ASD: left atrium and LV; VSD: right atrium and RV
ASD: right atrium and RV; VSD: isolated RV pressure loading without left-heart volume loading
ASD: isolated RV pressure loading; VSD: left atrium and LV
questions.explanation:
Chamber Loading in Congenital Left-to-Right Shunts

Correct answer: ASD: right atrium and RV; VSD: left atrium and LV

Follow the Recirculating Blood

**ASD: LA → RA/RV; primary right-heart volume load.**

**VSD/PDA: excess pulmonary flow returns to LA/LV; primary left-heart volume load.**

**Anomalous pulmonary venous drainage enters systemic veins and volume-loads the right heart.**

Separate Pressure and Volume

**A large VSD can transmit systemic pressure while also increasing pulmonary flow.**

A restrictive jet retains a pressure gradient; pressure does not quantify volume or PVR.

**Pulmonary stenosis causes RV pressure loading; pulmonary regurgitation causes RV volume loading without an ASD.**

**Advanced pulmonary vascular disease can reduce shunting and alter chamber patterns.**

Confirm anatomy/flow by echo and selected CMR; attribute chamber enlargement before intervention.

ASD: left atrium and LV; VSD: right atrium and RV: This reverses the usual pattern: ASD loads RA/RV, whereas VSD pulmonary recirculation returns excess volume to LA/LV.

ASD: right atrium and RV; VSD: isolated RV pressure loading without left-heart volume loading: Large VSD can transmit RV pressure, but significant left-to-right flow also increases LA/LV filling; it is not isolated RV pressure loading.

ASD: isolated RV pressure loading; VSD: left atrium and LV: Uncomplicated ASD predominantly increases RV filling volume; isolated RV pressure overload suggests another or additional mechanism.

questions.question: An adult with a secundum ASD has RV enlargement, wide fixed splitting of S2 and a grade 2/6 midsystolic murmur at the upper left sternal border. Doppler shows no valvar or subvalvar RV outflow obstruction. What principally generates this murmur?
options: Increased systolic flow across the pulmonary valve
High-velocity systolic flow through the atrial defect
Systolic regurgitation through the tricuspid valve
Dynamic systolic obstruction in the RV outflow tract
questions.explanation:
Atrial Shunting and the Pulmonary Flow Murmur

Correct answer: Increased systolic flow across the pulmonary valve

Atrial Shunt Physiology

**Pulmonary flow murmur: increased RV stroke volume across a normal pulmonary valve.**

The low-pressure atrial jet is usually inaudible; murmur loudness does not measure defect size.

**Fixed S2 splitting: persistent RV volume loading with buffered respiratory variation.**

A large shunt may also produce a tricuspid mid-diastolic flow rumble.

Assessment

**TTE: define the communication, RV enlargement and pulmonary pressure.**

Use TEE for device rims; CMR/CT for uncertain pulmonary veins or chamber measurements.

**Closure assessment: integrate shunt burden, PVR, anatomy and LV filling pressure.**

Atrial arrhythmias may persist after closure; advanced pulmonary vascular disease changes eligibility.

High-velocity systolic flow through the atrial defect: A high-pressure VSD jet can be loud. An uncomplicated ASD has a small atrial pressure gradient; its ejection murmur arises at the pulmonary valve.

Systolic regurgitation through the tricuspid valve: Tricuspid regurgitation produces a lower-sternal, usually holosystolic murmur. It does not explain this pulmonary-area midsystolic flow murmur.

Dynamic systolic obstruction in the RV outflow tract: RV outflow obstruction can produce an ejection murmur, but Doppler excludes it here; the ASD instead increases pulmonary flow.

questions.question: A 42-year-old with an interatrial left-to-right shunt has RV volume loading, PR 240 ms and a superior leftward QRS axis. Echocardiography also shows regurgitation through an abnormal left AV valve. Which defect best fits this combination?
options: Ostium primum defect in a partial AV septal defect
Ostium secundum defect at the fossa ovalis
Superior sinus venosus interatrial communication
Unroofed coronary sinus communication
questions.explanation:
Primum Communication and the Left Atrioventricular Valve

Correct answer: Ostium primum defect in a partial AV septal defect

Partial AV Septal Defect

**Primum communication + abnormal left AV valve + superior QRS axis.**

PR prolongation supports conduction involvement but is not diagnostic alone.

**Common AV junction: partial AVSD has separate valve orifices; complete AVSD adds a ventricular defect and common valve orifice.**

Strong association with trisomy 21; define anatomy directly.

**PFO differs from ASD: overlapping septal flaps form a tunnel without tissue deficiency.**

An incidental PFO rarely explains substantial chronic RV volume overload.

Repair and Follow-Up

**Echocardiography: map AV valves, shunt, LV outflow and pulmonary veins.**

Measure PVR invasively when pulmonary vascular disease is suspected.

**Indicated repair is generally surgical, addressing the septum and left AV valve.**

A conventional secundum device does not correct AVSD anatomy.

Follow residual valve regurgitation, shunts, outflow obstruction and conduction disease.

Communication | Important associated anatomy

Secundum | Fossa ovalis; assess device rims and pulmonary veins

Primum / partial AVSD | AV junction and left AV-valve abnormality

Sinus venosus | Caval–pulmonary venous junction; frequently anomalous pulmonary venous connection

Unroofed coronary sinus | Coronary sinus roof; assess persistent left SVC

Ostium secundum defect at the fossa ovalis: Secundum defects cause RV loading, often with incomplete RBBB/right axis. The superior axis and abnormal left AV valve favor partial AVSD.

Superior sinus venosus interatrial communication: Sinus venosus defects commonly accompany anomalous pulmonary venous drainage. They do not explain the characteristic AV-valve and superior-axis combination.

Unroofed coronary sinus communication: Unroofed coronary sinus may accompany a persistent left SVC. The supplied valve and electrical findings instead support primum anatomy.

questions.question: A woman with an unchanged unrepaired secundum ASD develops hypertension-associated LV hypertrophy over two decades. Her LVEF remains normal, but LV filling pressure rises and left-to-right shunting increases. Pulmonary vascular resistance remains low. Which change most directly explains the increased shunt?
options: Reduced RV diastolic compliance
Reduced LV diastolic compliance
Increased pulmonary vascular resistance
Increased LV diastolic compliance
questions.explanation:
Ventricular Compliance and Atrial Shunt Magnitude

Correct answer: Reduced LV diastolic compliance

Compliance and Shunt Direction

**Reduced LV compliance raises LA pressure and increases left-to-right atrial flow.**

The defect can remain unchanged; preserved LVEF does not exclude diastolic dysfunction.

**RV stiffness or rising PVR can reduce or reverse left-to-right flow.**

Before Closure

**Assess BP, volume status, AV-valve disease and LV filling pressure.**

**Treat reversible contributors, then reassess complete closure, fenestration or deferral.**

**Selected balloon occlusion: 2025 Class 2b.**

May overestimate the wedge-pressure rise after actual device closure; not a validated pass/fail test.

LV stiffness ↑ → LA pressure ↑ → Left-to-right shunt ↑ → Closure may unmask pulmonary congestion

Reduced RV diastolic compliance: A stiff RV resists filling and tends to reduce left-to-right shunting; the supplied change originates in the LV.

Increased pulmonary vascular resistance: Rising PVR can reduce or reverse flow, but PVR remains low here and left-to-right shunting increases.

Increased LV diastolic compliance: Improved LV compliance lowers filling pressure and favors LV filling; it is the opposite of the documented hypertensive change.

questions.explanation:
Caval Oximetry and Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Drainage

Correct answer: A right pulmonary vein draining into the SVC

Localize the First Step-Up

**Lower-SVC oxygen enrichment suggests pulmonary venous entry into the SVC.**

Repeat samples and confirm position: streaming or contamination can mislead.

Do not use an enriched lower-SVC sample as pre-shunt mixed venous blood.

Map and Treat the Connection

**TEE plus CMR/CT: map all pulmonary veins, caval junctions and atrial septum.**

**Quantify Qp/Qs and RV volume burden; the step-up alone does not prove a sinus venosus defect.**

**Significant suitable lesions: surgical repair or selected expert covered-stent correction.**

Covered-stent evidence is mainly observational; test-balloon assessment must confirm unobstructed pulmonary venous redirection.

Monitor SVC/pulmonary venous obstruction and residual shunting.

questions.question: An adult with a suspected atrial-level left-to-right shunt has RV enlargement that is difficult to quantify by TTE. The clinical team needs reproducible RV volumes and pulmonary-to-systemic flow assessment. Which examination most directly combines these measurements?

Cine CMR volumetry with anatomy-specific phase-contrast flow assessment
Right-heart catheterization with an oximetry run
questions.explanation:
CMR Shunt Quantification and Right Ventricular Volumes

Correct answer: Cine CMR volumetry with anatomy-specific phase-contrast flow assessment

What CMR Measures

**Phase-contrast flow** quantifies pulmonary and systemic forward flow to calculate Qp/Qs.

**Volumetric imaging** measures RV size and systolic function without geometric assumptions; anatomical sequences map pulmonary venous connections.

Selecting and Interpreting Tests

**Technical checks:** measurement planes, velocity encoding, arrhythmia, regurgitation and collateral flow can alter flow estimates.

**Echocardiography** assesses valves and shunt anatomy; TEE better defines septal rims when device closure is considered.

**Catheterization** measures pressures and calculates PVR when pulmonary vascular disease or uncertain operability requires invasive clarification. CMR flow alone cannot supply these pressures.

TEE septal imaging with a contrast shunt study: TEE can define the septal defect and contrast passage, but that primarily anatomic assessment does not replace the requested comprehensive RV volumes and quantitative pulmonary/systemic flows.

Three-dimensional TTE ventricular volumetry with repeat Doppler flow estimates: Three-dimensional echo can improve RV measurement when image quality is adequate, but the stated difficult transthoracic quantification favors CMR for reproducible volumes and integrated flows.

Right-heart catheterization with an oximetry run: Catheterization can quantify shunting and is important for pressure or resistance questions, but does not directly provide the reproducible RV volumetry requested alongside flow assessment.

questions.explanation:
ASD Closure for Right-Ventricular Volume Overload

Correct answer: Refer for anatomically appropriate ASD closure

2025 ACC/AHA Closure Criteria

**Unrepaired ASD: Qp:Qs ≥1.5 + RV dilation + PVR ==≤2 Wood units== + no significant LV disease.**

Symptoms are not required when these favorable criteria are met.

ESC 2020 uses a different low-PVR category (==<3 Wood units==); do not merge frameworks.

Closure and Follow-Up

**Confirm anatomy: defect size, rims, adjacent structures and pulmonary veins.**

**Suitable secundum ASD: prefer transcatheter closure.**

AVSD/primum or unsuitable anatomy generally requires surgery.

**After device closure: ESC 2020 specifies antiplatelet therapy for ≥6 months, aspirin ==≥75 mg==/day.**

Individualize for bleeding, allergy and other antithrombotic indications.

**Image device position, residual shunt and RV remodeling.**

Monitor thrombus and atrial arrhythmias; closure does not erase established rhythm substrate.

Start PAH-targeted treatment before reconsidering closure: PAH treatment is used for selected elevated-PVR pathways. PVR 1.6 Wood units does not justify preparatory PAH medication.

Continue surveillance until exercise symptoms develop: Observation suits a small shunt without important RV loading. This asymptomatic patient already meets favorable hemodynamic closure criteria.

Use chronic diuretics to reduce the need for closure: Diuretics relieve congestion but do not remove the persistent shunt; they are not definitive treatment for this suitable significant ASD.

ASD With PAH: Response to Therapy and Closure Reassessment

Correct answer: Closure can be considered by the ACHD/PH team with ongoing PAH follow-up

Selected Treat-and-Reassess Pathway

**2025 ASD pathway: initial PVR ==5–8 Wood units== falling below 5 on PAH therapy may permit closure.**

Require significant left-to-right flow, RV dilation and no important LV disease.

Repeat invasive hemodynamics; a lower echo-estimated pressure is insufficient.

**ACHD/PH team selects complete closure, fenestration or nonclosure.**

Selected-responder cohorts do not prove universal reversibility or cure.

Drug Examples and Monitoring

**Sildenafil: ==20 mg== orally three times daily.**

Do not combine with organic nitrates or riociguat; monitor BP.

**Macitentan: ==10 mg== orally daily.**

Pregnancy contraindicated; assess contraception, hemoglobin, liver status and fluid retention.

**Continue PAH surveillance after closure; treatment may still be required.**

PAH treatment → Repeat PVR and shunt assessment → Expert closure decision → Long-term PAH follow-up

Closure should be paired with planned discontinuation of PAH therapy: Closure removes the shunt but may leave pulmonary vascular disease; it does not justify planned withdrawal of PAH therapy.

Closure assessment should wait until PVR reaches 2 Wood units or less: PVR ≤2 defines the uncomplicated pathway. Selected treated responders below 5 may still undergo specialist closure assessment.

The baseline PVR establishes Eisenmenger physiology and favors nonclosure: Elevated baseline PVR alone is not Eisenmenger syndrome. Net left-to-right flow, normal resting saturation and response require separate assessment.

questions.question: An adult has a left-to-right restrictive VSD with peak Doppler velocity 4.5 m/s. Simultaneous systolic systemic BP is 125 mmHg. There is no LV outflow or aortic obstruction. Using the simplified Bernoulli equation, what is the estimated RV systolic pressure?

questions.explanation:
Restrictive VSD: Doppler Gradient Versus RV Pressure

Correct answer: 44 mmHg

Calculate RV Pressure

**VSD gradient = 4v² = 4 × 4.5² = ==81 mmHg==.**

**No LV outflow obstruction: LV systolic pressure ≈ systemic pressure = ==125 mmHg==.**

**Left-to-right jet: RV systolic pressure = 125 − 81 = ==44 mmHg==.**

Interpretation and Limits

**The jet measures a pressure difference, not shunt volume.**

A restrictive defect can produce a loud high-velocity murmur despite limited volume overload.

**Check Doppler alignment and the systemic-pressure measurement.**

LV outflow obstruction invalidates simple substitution of systemic BP for LV pressure.

**RV pressure approximates PA pressure only without RV outflow obstruction.**

PVR requires pulmonary flow and mean PA/wedge pressures; this calculation cannot diagnose pulmonary vascular disease.

Correct answer: Seek ACHD surgical review of VSD closure and valve preservation

**Outlet and some perimembranous VSDs undermine aortic cusp support.**

Prolapse may partly restrict the defect while worsening aortic regurgitation.

**Define cusp injury, AR progression, LV size/function and pulmonary vascular status.**

questions.explanation:
VSD Closure: Left-Heart Volume Load and Lesion-Specific Risk

Correct answer: Qp:Qs 1.8 with progressive LV dilatation attributable to the VSD

Hemodynamic Closure Indication

**Low PVR + Qp:Qs ≥1.5 + important/progressive LV dilation attributable to the VSD.**

Excess pulmonary flow returns to the LA/LV; ASD instead primarily volume-loads the RA/RV.

**Confirm attribution: exclude primary cardiomyopathy or valve disease.**

Murmur intensity, diameter and preserved EF do not quantify shunt burden.

Additional Indications and Procedure

**Progressive VSD-related AR and selected recent VSD-associated endocarditis may justify closure.**

Preventing a first IE episode alone is not an indication.

**Select surgery or catheter closure from anatomy, valve involvement and conduction risk.**

**Elevated PVR requires a separate pathway; Eisenmenger physiology precludes closure.**

Follow residual shunt, ventricular remodeling, valves and AV conduction.

ASD | RA and RV | Pulmonary flow murmur; assess atrial and pulmonary venous anatomy

VSD | LA and LV | Jet velocity measures an LV–RV pressure difference, not shunt volume

PDA | LA and LV | Continuous flow requires a persistent aortopulmonary gradient

Correct answer: The usefulness of VSD closure remains uncertain and requires specialist assessment

**Qp:Qs ≥1.5; initial PVR ==5–8 Wood units==; no hypoxemia; treated PVR <5.**

**Do not transfer the more favorable selected-ASD recommendation to VSD.**

Different pressure loading and evidence bases matter.

**Repeat invasive flow/resistance assessment; review ventricular function, oxygenation and anatomy.**

**Continue risk-directed PAH therapy and surveillance.**

A lower resistance does not prove cure or justify stopping treatment.

**Consider intervention only after individualized ACHD/PH discussion.**

Small series or fenestration feasibility do not prove universal survival benefit; established Eisenmenger remains a nonclosure setting.

questions.explanation:
Perimembranous VSD and the AV Conduction Axis

Correct answer: The AV conduction axis near the posteroinferior defect margin

AV Conduction Anatomy

**The AV conduction axis lies near the posteroinferior margin of a typical perimembranous VSD.**

Device compression, injury or later tissue reaction may produce complete AV block.

**Risk depends on defect type, tissue margins, device design/sizing and valve proximity.**

Procedure and Monitoring

**Map valves and defect anatomy; obtain a baseline ECG.**

**Choose surgery when associated aortic-valve disease or anatomy favors repair.**

**Monitor immediate and delayed conduction changes.**

New PR prolongation, bundle-branch change, syncope or bradycardia requires assessment.

Significant high-grade block needs rhythm monitoring and temporary/permanent pacing assessment according to persistence and clinical status.

**Also assess residual shunt, hemolysis, infection risk and ventricular load.**

The left posterior fascicle in the inferoposterior LV septum: Isolated posterior fascicular injury affects activation/axis. The adjacent proximal AV conduction axis is the relevant complete-block hazard.

The distal right bundle branch after bundle bifurcation: Isolated distal right-bundle injury causes RBBB, not interruption of conduction to both ventricles through the proximal AV axis.

The left anterior fascicle in the anterosuperior LV septum: Left anterior fascicular injury changes axis and intraventricular activation; it does not explain the principal complete-AV-block risk.

questions.question: An adult with a substantial left-to-right PDA has bounding pulses and a continuous infraclavicular murmur. Which chamber-loading pattern is most characteristic of the shunt itself?

questions.explanation:
Ductal Runoff and Left-Heart Volume Loading

Correct answer: Left atrial and left ventricular volume loading

Ductal Recirculation

**Aorta → pulmonary artery → lungs → LA/LV: primary left-heart volume loading.**

Diastolic runoff produces bounding pulses and widened pulse pressure.

**Continuous murmur requires an aortopulmonary gradient in systole and diastole.**

Advanced pulmonary vascular disease can reduce its diastolic component.

Investigation and Treatment

**TTE: ductal flow, LA/LV size and pulmonary pressure.**

CT/CMR clarifies complex adult anatomy; catheterization assesses uncertain PVR/closure tolerance.

**Suitable significant left-to-right PDA with favorable PVR: catheter closure.**

Right-to-left Eisenmenger physiology requires nonclosure and specialist PAH care.

**Differentiate coronary fistula, aortopulmonary window and systemic AV fistula by entry site and chamber load.**

Aortic runoff → Pulmonary flow ↑ → Pulmonary venous return ↑ → LA/LV volume load ↑

Right atrial and right ventricular volume loading: RA/RV volume loading is typical of an atrial-level shunt. A PDA primarily recirculates blood through the LA/LV.

Isolated right ventricular pressure loading with normal pulmonary flow: Isolated RV pressure overload suggests obstruction or pulmonary vascular disease; uncomplicated PDA initially increases pulmonary flow and LV volume.

Isolated left atrial pressure loading without LV volume recirculation: Mitral inflow obstruction primarily raises LA pressure. PDA flow passes through the LA into the LV, creating volume recirculation.

questions.explanation:
Differential Cyanosis in Ductal Pulmonary Vascular Disease

Correct answer: Patent ductus arteriosus with advanced pulmonary vascular disease

Differential Cyanosis

**Right-to-left PDA flow enters the descending aorta beyond the usual left subclavian origin.**

Hands remain better oxygenated; feet develop desaturation and clubbing.

**Measure both upper- and lower-limb saturation.**

Unusual arch anatomy or additional connections can alter the distribution.

Assess Before Considering Closure

**Define ductal direction, pulmonary resistance and ventricular function with imaging and selected catheterization.**

**Established ductal Eisenmenger: do not close the pressure-relief pathway.**

questions.explanation:
Adult PDA: Selecting Definitive Closure

Correct answer: Transcatheter PDA device closure

When and How to Close

**Attributable progressive LA/LV enlargement + net left-to-right flow + favorable PVR supports closure.**

**Prefer percutaneous closure when technically feasible.**

Assess morphology, calcification, adjacent vessels and device-related obstruction risk.

Surgery suits unsuitable catheter anatomy or associated surgical lesions.

**Monitor residual flow, hemolysis, device position and adjacent PA/aortic obstruction.**

**Follow LV size/function as recirculating volume falls.**

**Selected left-to-right PDA with PVR ==2–5 Wood units==: discuss with PH experts.**

Test occlusion may help; symptoms, rising PA pressure or falling aortic pressure suggest intolerance.

No universal test-occlusion cutoff; do not extrapolate to right-to-left Eisenmenger physiology.

questions.question: A 34-year-old had surgical coarctation repair in childhood. TTE shows preserved LV function and no large residual gradient, but the repair site is incompletely visualized. There has been no cross-sectional aortic imaging for many years. Which study most comprehensively assesses the repair segment, arch and collateral anatomy?

TTE with repeated suprasternal Doppler sweeps alone
TEE limited to the descending thoracic aorta
Duplex ultrasound of the abdominal aorta and renal arteries
questions.explanation:
Thoracic Aortic Surveillance After Coarctation Repair

Correct answer: CMR angiography of the thoracic aorta including the repair site

Image the Aorta, Not Only the Gradient

**CMR maps arch geometry, repair site, collaterals and aneurysm without radiation.**

CTA is an alternative; stent artifact or integrity assessment may favor CT.

**A normal Doppler gradient does not exclude repair-site aneurysm.**

Assess root/ascending aorta and associated bicuspid valve disease.

Lifelong Surveillance

**Check arm/leg BP, LV remodeling, valves and symptoms.**

Ambulatory BP or exercise testing can reveal masked pressure burden.

**ESC 2024: CT/CMR every 3–5 years, adjusted for anatomy and prior findings.**

Residual narrowing, dilation or new symptoms require earlier evaluation.

**2025: brain MR/CT angiographic aneurysm screening may be considered.**

Individualize by age, hypertension and preferences; thoracic imaging does not screen the brain.

questions.question: An adult has arm BP 166/92 mmHg, leg BP 154/86 mmHg and an invasive coarctation peak-to-peak gradient of 12 mmHg. CTA shows a 7-mm isthmus, a 20-mm descending aorta at the diaphragm and extensive intercostal collaterals. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The modest arm–leg pressure difference makes hypertension unrelated to coarctation
The catheter gradient establishes that the anatomical narrowing is minor
The maximum instantaneous Doppler gradient can replace the catheter value directly
Important obstruction remains possible because collateral flow can reduce the measured gradient
questions.explanation:
Severe Coarctation With a Modest Measured Gradient

Correct answer: Important obstruction remains possible because collateral flow can reduce the measured gradient

Why a Low Gradient Can Mislead

**Collaterals bypass the narrowing and reduce measured pressure drop.**

Low cardiac output or severe aortic stenosis can also attenuate the gradient.

**Isthmus ratio = 7/20 = 0.35: substantial anatomical narrowing.**

A ratio below 0.5 is a conventional major-narrowing marker, not an isolated intervention command.

Integrated Assessment

**Combine hypertension, LV load, symptoms, cross-sectional anatomy and stated gradient type.**

Doppler maximum instantaneous and catheter peak-to-peak values are not interchangeable.

**Radiofemoral delay and inferior rib notching reflect chronic obstruction/collaterals.**

Notching typically involves ribs 3–8; pre/poststenotic contours can form a figure-of-3 sign.

**Severe anatomy with consequences merits ACHD repair assessment despite a 12-mmHg gradient.**

Assessment | 2025 significance finding or case calculation | Qualification

Arm–leg systolic BP difference | Above ==20 mmHg== | Collateral flow can attenuate the difference

Invasive peak-to-peak gradient | Above ==20 mmHg== | Flow and loading conditions affect the value

Doppler mean systolic gradient | Above ==20 mmHg== | Do not substitute the maximum instantaneous value

Isthmus / diaphragm-level descending aorta | 7/20 = 0.35 in this case | Anatomical severity complements physiological assessment

The catheter gradient establishes that the anatomical narrowing is minor: Gradient depends on flow; extensive collaterals can conceal severe anatomical narrowing despite a low catheter measurement.

The maximum instantaneous Doppler gradient can replace the catheter value directly: Maximum instantaneous Doppler and catheter peak-to-peak gradients measure different pressure relationships and cannot be substituted directly.

questions.question: A 28-year-old with hypertension has discrete native coarctation, an invasive peak-to-peak gradient of 32 mmHg and suitable landing zones and arterial access. Surgical interposition graft repair
Endovascular stent repair of the narrowed segment
questions.explanation:
Adult Native Coarctation: Choosing a Repair Approach

Correct answer: Endovascular stent repair of the narrowed segment

Select the Repair

**Hypertension + significant obstruction + suitable landing zones/access favors adult stent repair.**

Covered stents are often preferred; anatomy determines device selection.

**Map arch, branch vessels, aneurysms, collaterals and access arteries.**

Risks and Follow-Up

**Discuss aortic injury/aneurysm, migration/fracture, access complications and reintervention.**

**Surgery remains appropriate for complex arch disease, unsuitable landing zones or combined lesions.**

**Repair does not guarantee normal BP: continue treatment and imaging.**

Surgical ascending-to-descending aortic bypass: Ascending-to-descending bypass can treat complex arch disease. It is not the usual first repair for this discrete stent-suitable lesion.

Coarctation: Doppler and Catheter Gradients

Correct answer: The Doppler mean systolic gradient

Doppler Versus Catheter Measurement

**Doppler mean systolic gradient best approximates catheter peak-to-peak gradient in the 2025 framework.**

**Catheter peak-to-peak compares separate systolic peaks; Doppler maximum uses an instantaneous difference.**

The relationship is empirical; values are not identical in every patient.

Avoid Misclassification After Repair

**High Doppler gradient without narrowing: consider compliance and pressure recovery.**

**Low gradient despite narrowing: consider collaterals or low output.**

**Correlate with CT/CMR anatomy, LV function, arm/leg BP and symptoms.**

Account for proximal velocity and Doppler alignment; state the measured index.

Do not select reintervention from a single peak velocity; continue aneurysm and hypertension surveillance.

The proximal-velocity-corrected maximum instantaneous gradient: Proximal-velocity correction reduces one error but leaves a maximum instantaneous index, distinct from the catheter peak-to-peak measurement.

The uncorrected maximum instantaneous systolic gradient: Maximum instantaneous gradient can exceed peak-to-peak pressure difference; it is not the closest named Doppler approximation.

The maximum gradient derived from the diastolic flow tail: A diastolic flow tail supports obstruction, but its peak gradient is not the systolic index used for this approximation.

The leaflets are thin and mobile, the annulus is normal-sized, and there is no important pulmonary regurgitation or subvalvular obstruction. Which intervention is preferred?
options: Transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement
Surgical pulmonary valve replacement as the first procedure
Surgical pulmonary valvotomy as the initial procedure
Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty
questions.explanation:
Balloon Treatment of Suitable Valvular Pulmonary Stenosis

Correct answer: Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty

Severity and Anatomy

**Severe valvar pulmonary stenosis:** peak velocity >4 m/s or maximum instantaneous Doppler gradient >64 mmHg; mild <3 m/s, moderate 3–4 m/s.

**This patient:** 4 × 4.5² = 81 mmHg. Doppler instantaneous and catheter peak-to-peak gradients are not interchangeable.

**Mobile doming leaflets** and a normal annulus favor balloon commissurotomy. Dysplastic valves, including those associated with Noonan syndrome, respond less predictably.

Treatment and Follow-up

**Balloon valvuloplasty** is preferred for symptomatic moderate/severe valvar obstruction with favorable anatomy in the 2025 ACHD framework.

**Surgery** suits unsuitable anatomy, substantial regurgitation or failed balloon treatment; choose repair versus replacement individually.

**Follow-up:** residual gradient, pulmonary regurgitation, RV size/function and exercise response.

**A pulmonary ejection click** may soften or merge with S1 on inspiration; distinguish this from the murmur.

Transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement: Transcatheter replacement is valuable for selected dysfunctional conduits, bioprostheses and repaired RV outflow tracts. This patient has a native, mobile doming valve that can be opened by balloon commissurotomy; implanting a prosthesis is not the preferred initial treatment.

Surgical pulmonary valve replacement as the first procedure: Surgery is appropriate for unsuitable anatomy, failed balloon treatment or important associated lesions, but a suitable isolated doming valve generally favors balloon valvuloplasty.

Surgical pulmonary valvotomy as the initial procedure: Surgical relief is relevant when anatomy is unsuitable for catheter treatment or associated lesions require operation; favorable isolated doming valvular stenosis generally supports balloon treatment first.

questions.question: An adult with a small perimembranous VSD has exertional limitation. Catheter pullback shows PA systolic pressure 24 mmHg, distal RV systolic pressure 26 mmHg and proximal RV systolic pressure 78 mmHg. The pulmonary valve is structurally normal. Which obstruction best fits the pressure distribution?
options: Intracavitary obstruction from a double-chambered right ventricle
Valvar pulmonary stenosis
Supravalvar main pulmonary artery stenosis
Peripheral branch pulmonary artery stenosis
questions.explanation:
Intracavitary RV Pressure Step and Double-Chambered RV

Correct answer: Intracavitary obstruction from a double-chambered right ventricle

Localize the Pressure Step

**Proximal RV 78 → distal RV 26 → PA ==24 mmHg==: obstruction is within the RV.**

Double-chambered RV has obstructing muscle bundles, often with a perimembranous VSD.

**Define whether the VSD enters the high- or low-pressure compartment.**

TTE may miss the full partition; CMR/CT and selected catheterization clarify anatomy.

Treatment

**Symptomatic moderate-or-greater DCRV obstruction: surgical muscle-bundle repair.**

Assess associated VSD, valves, ventricular function and arrhythmia.

**Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty does not remove muscular intracavitary obstruction.**

**Severe asymptomatic obstruction also merits expert review.**

Follow residual/recurrent obstruction and RV remodeling; high proximal RV pressure is not automatically PAH.

Valvar pulmonary stenosis: Valvar PS creates a distal-RV-to-PA step. Here those pressures nearly match; the major step is proximal within the RV.

Supravalvar main pulmonary artery stenosis: Supravalvar stenosis is beyond the valve and raises upstream outflow pressure; it does not explain the intracavitary partition.

Peripheral branch pulmonary artery stenosis: Branch PA stenosis requires main-to-branch pressure/anatomical assessment. It does not primarily divide the RV into two pressure chambers.

questions.question: A 41-year-old has a bicuspid aortic valve and a 4.6-cm ascending aorta. His asymptomatic first-degree relatives have normal cardiac examinations. Which initial family-screening strategy best follows the 2022 ACC/AHA aortic guideline?
options: Resting ECG and ambulatory BP without structural imaging
TTE to assess the valve, aortic root and ascending aorta
Thoracic CTA as the first test for every relative
Genetic testing first, with imaging restricted to variant carriers
questions.explanation:
Bicuspid Valve Aortopathy and First-Degree Relatives

Correct answer: TTE to assess the valve, aortic root and ascending aorta

Family Screening

**2022 ACC/AHA: first-degree relatives need TTE when BAV coexists with aortic dilation.**

Assess valve morphology/function, root and ascending aorta.

Aortopathy may occur with a tricuspid valve; normal examination is insufficient.

**Incomplete TTE visualization: complete imaging with CT or MRI.**

Proband: Aortic Intervention Thresholds

**==4.6 cm== alone does not mandate isolated replacement; assess growth and risk.**

Rapid BAV growth: ==≥0.3 cm== in one year.

Risk modifiers: family dissection, coarctation, root phenotype and body size.

**2022 ACC/AHA: operate at ==5.5 cm==; selected earlier surgery at ==5.0–5.4 cm== with additional risk.**

Area/height ==≥10 cm²/m== can support intervention.

==≥4.5 cm== may justify concomitant replacement during aortic valve surgery; it is not a universal isolated-surgery threshold.

Resting ECG and ambulatory BP without structural imaging: ECG and BP can identify other problems but cannot exclude bicuspid morphology or silent aortic enlargement.

Thoracic CTA as the first test for every relative: CTA is useful when echo is incomplete or specific anatomy requires it; TTE is the initial family-screening test.

Genetic testing first, with imaging restricted to variant carriers: Genetic testing helps selected heritable disease, but many BAV families lack an identified variant; imaging cannot be restricted to carriers.

questions.question: An adult with unrepaired TOF and a large nonrestrictive VSD becomes more cyanotic after systemic vasodilation. RV outflow obstruction has not changed. Which hemodynamic change best explains the desaturation?
options: Lower systemic resistance increases the LV-to-RV gradient across a restrictive VSD
Lower systemic resistance favors right-to-left flow through the VSD
Lower systemic resistance directly relieves the fixed RV outflow obstruction
Lower systemic resistance reduces the proportion of RV output entering the aorta
questions.explanation:
Systemic Resistance and Right-to-Left Flow in Unrepaired TOF

Correct answer: Lower systemic resistance favors right-to-left flow through the VSD

Unrepaired TOF Hemodynamics

**Large VSD + RV outflow obstruction permit competing pulmonary and systemic ejection routes.**

**Lower SVR makes systemic ejection easier: right-to-left shunt increases and saturation falls.**

The obstruction need not change; raising SVR can reduce shunting in an appropriate acute setting.

Anatomy and Clinical Implications

**Four components: malalignment VSD, RV outflow obstruction, overriding aorta and RV hypertrophy.**

**Murmur usually comes from outflow obstruction, not the large low-gradient VSD.**

A quieter murmur during deterioration may mean less pulmonary flow.

**Assess oxygenation, vascular tone, hydration and filling during acute deterioration.**

Seek congenital expertise and definitive anatomical assessment; repaired-TOF scar/regurgitation physiology differs.

Systemic resistance ↓ → RV-to-aorta ejection favored → Right-to-left flow ↑ → Systemic saturation ↓

Lower systemic resistance increases the LV-to-RV gradient across a restrictive VSD: Restrictive defects produce pressure-gradient-limited jets. This large nonrestrictive TOF VSD permits pressure communication and systemic diversion.

Lower systemic resistance directly relieves the fixed RV outflow obstruction: Systemic arteriolar dilation does not remove fixed valvar or muscular RV outflow obstruction; pulmonary flow need not increase.

Lower systemic resistance reduces the proportion of RV output entering the aorta: Less RV-to-aorta diversion would improve saturation. With obstruction, lower SVR instead favors more desaturated systemic ejection.

questions.question: An asymptomatic adult with repaired tetralogy of Fallot has moderate-to-severe pulmonary regurgitation. CMR shows RV end-systolic volume index 92 mL/m² and RVEF 43%; serial exercise testing shows declining capacity. Under the 2025 ACC/AHA ACHD framework, which approach is appropriate?
options: Repeat CMR and exercise testing in twelve months
Trial heart-failure medication before reconsidering valve referral
Complete electrophysiological risk stratification before valve referral
Assess pulmonary valve replacement through the ACHD valve team
questions.explanation:
Pulmonary Regurgitation After Repaired Tetralogy Requires RV Assessment

Correct answer: Assess pulmonary valve replacement through the ACHD valve team

2025 Pulmonary Valve Replacement Framework

**Asymptomatic repaired TOF:** moderate or greater pulmonary valve dysfunction plus at least two adverse markers supports replacement assessment.

**Qualifying markers:** RVESVi >80 mL/m²; RVEDV ≥2 × LVEDV; RVEF ≤46%; LVEF ≤50%; progressive objective exercise decline.

**This patient has three:** RVESVi 92 mL/m², RVEF 43% and declining exercise performance. Reported absence of symptoms does not negate objective deterioration.

Valve-team Assessment

**Define anatomy** and associated lesions; choose surgical or transcatheter replacement according to RVOT suitability and coronary relationships.

**Assess arrhythmia risk alongside valve planning.** Replacement improves hemodynamics but does not eliminate scar-related ventricular tachycardia.

**Continue surveillance** of ventricular function, residual valve dysfunction, exercise capacity and rhythm after intervention.

Repeat CMR and exercise testing in twelve months: Serial imaging and exercise testing are appropriate when findings remain stable and intervention criteria are not met. Here RVESVi 92 mL/m², RVEF 43% and progressive exercise decline already provide three qualifying markers; another annual observation interval should not replace referral now.

Trial heart-failure medication before reconsidering valve referral: Medication may be needed for coexisting ventricular failure or congestion. It does not correct pulmonary regurgitation, and a mandatory drug trial is not part of the specified valve-replacement pathway. The supplied structural and functional findings warrant valve assessment without that prerequisite.

Complete electrophysiological risk stratification before valve referral: Electrophysiological assessment can guide VT ablation and sudden-death prevention in selected repaired-TOF patients and may be coordinated with valve planning. It is not a prerequisite to referring a patient who already meets the hemodynamic replacement framework; electrical and valve evaluation can proceed together.

questions.question: A 39-year-old with repaired TOF and an old RVOT patch has sustained monomorphic VT. CMR shows fibrosis near the patch and ventricular septal repair. Which mechanism most commonly explains this arrhythmia substrate?
options: Macroreentry through slow-conducting anatomical isthmuses
cAMP-mediated triggered activity in an otherwise structurally normal RVOT
Bundle-branch reentry using the His–Purkinje system as the principal circuit
Enhanced automaticity from a single normal Purkinje focus
questions.explanation:
Monomorphic VT After TOF Repair

Correct answer: Macroreentry through slow-conducting anatomical isthmuses

Scar-Related Macroreentry

**Patches, scars and valve annuli form fixed circuit boundaries; slow-conducting isthmuses sustain monomorphic VT.**

A key isthmus lies between the pulmonary annulus and VSD patch.

**Risk assessment integrates clinical VT/syncope, CMR scar and ventricular function.**

QRS ==≥180 ms== is a historical marker, not a stand-alone ICD rule.

Coordinated Treatment

**Congenital EP mapping identifies the critical isthmus for ablation.**

**Assess residual pulmonary valve dysfunction and ventricular loading concurrently.**

**Individualize ICD treatment from presentation, reversible causes and overall risk.**

Selected tolerated VT may have an ablation-led pathway in expert care.

Successful ablation or valve replacement does not eliminate every future arrhythmic risk.

cAMP-mediated triggered activity in an otherwise structurally normal RVOT: Triggered activity underlies idiopathic RVOT VT, often without scar; the supplied repaired-TOF substrate favors anatomical macroreentry.

Bundle-branch reentry using the His–Purkinje system as the principal circuit: Bundle-branch reentry occurs with selected His–Purkinje disease; postrepair RBBB alone does not establish it as the dominant circuit.

Enhanced automaticity from a single normal Purkinje focus: Focal automatic rhythms occur in other contexts but do not explain the common patch/isthmus-related sustained reentrant substrate.

questions.question: An adult with repaired TOF has worsening exercise tolerance. CMR pulmonary regurgitant fraction is 12%, but imaging shows substantial RVOT obstruction. RV systolic pressure is 90 mmHg while systemic systolic pressure is 120 mmHg; distal PA pressure is not elevated. Which next approach is most appropriate?
options: Begin medical treatment for RV failure and reassess the obstruction after optimization
Repeat CMR after an interval to establish progressive RV volume enlargement
Undertake pulmonary vasodilator testing to guide PAH-directed treatment
Refer for assessment of relief of the residual RVOT obstruction
questions.explanation:
Pressure-Loaded RV After TOF Repair

Correct answer: Refer for assessment of relief of the residual RVOT obstruction

Pressure Load Despite Little Regurgitation

**RV/systemic systolic pressure = 90/120 = 0.75, exceeding two-thirds systemic.**

Low regurgitant fraction does not negate important obstructive dysfunction.

**Normal distal PA pressure localizes the pressure load to the RV outflow pathway.**

High RV pressure is not PAH when intervening obstruction is present.

Intervention Assessment

**Map valvar, muscular, conduit or branch-artery obstruction and its severity.**

**Assess ventricular function, TR, rhythm and objective exercise change.**

**Select catheter relief, valve intervention or surgery according to anatomy.**

Symptoms with important obstruction do not require waiting for severe PR or RV volume progression.

**Follow residual gradient, new PR and RV response; scar-related rhythm risk persists.**

Begin medical treatment for RV failure and reassess the obstruction after optimization: Medication can optimize congestion but cannot relieve a fixed lesion; it should not impose a prerequisite delay before anatomical assessment.

Repeat CMR after an interval to establish progressive RV volume enlargement: Serial CMR suits uncertain stable indications. Symptoms and major pressure loading already warrant intervention assessment without proving further volume enlargement.

Undertake pulmonary vasodilator testing to guide PAH-directed treatment: Vasodilator testing addresses selected pulmonary vascular disease. Normal distal PA pressure and an RVOT pressure step identify mechanical obstruction here.

questions.question: A 34-year-old with a large unrepaired VSD had pulmonary overcirculation in childhood. Current catheterization shows mean PA pressure 75 mmHg, wedge pressure 10 mmHg, PVR 18 Wood units and Qp/Qs 0.8. Systemic saturation is 82%, with bidirectional flow and no RV outflow obstruction. Which PAH-CHD category best fits?
options: PAH associated with a small coincidental defect
Eisenmenger syndrome
PAH persisting after correction of a congenital defect
PAH with a prevalent systemic-to-pulmonary shunt
questions.explanation:
Eisenmenger Syndrome Within PAH Associated With Congenital Shunts

Correct answer: Eisenmenger syndrome

Eisenmenger Physiology

**Longstanding large shunt → pulmonary arteriolar remodeling → high PVR → bidirectional/right-to-left flow.**

Earlier overcirculation and the causal large VSD distinguish this from coincidental-defect PAH.

**2022 ESC/ERS precapillary PH: mPAP ==>20 mmHg==, PAWP ==≤15 mmHg==, PVR ==>2 Wood units==.**

These hemodynamics alone do not establish Eisenmenger syndrome.

**PVR = (mPAP − PAWP)/Qp; use mmHg and L/min.**

In shunts, pulmonary flow Qp is not interchangeable with systemic flow Qs.

Clinical Consequences

**Do not close the established Eisenmenger pressure-relief pathway: RV failure may follow.**

**ACHD/PH care: targeted therapy, exercise/functional assessment, iron and renal monitoring.**

Assess bleeding, arrhythmia, embolism and infection; pregnancy risk is very high.

Exclude air meticulously from IV lines because systemic embolization is possible.

PAH-CHD group | Distinguishing context

Eisenmenger | Large causal shunt with advanced pulmonary vascular disease and reversal

Prevalent systemic-to-pulmonary shunt | Predominantly left-to-right flow remains

Small/coincidental defect | Defect insufficient to explain the pulmonary vascular disease

After correction | PAH persists or develops after anatomical repair

PAH associated with a small coincidental defect: Coincidental small defects do not explain the arteriopathy. This large longstanding VSD caused prior overcirculation and subsequent reversal.

PAH persisting after correction of a congenital defect: Post-correction PAH requires prior repair; this defect remains open and carries desaturated systemic flow.

PAH with a prevalent systemic-to-pulmonary shunt: Prevalent systemic-to-pulmonary shunts retain net left-to-right flow. Qp/Qs 0.8 with cyanosis instead supports Eisenmenger physiology.

questions.question: A stable adult with Eisenmenger syndrome has hemoglobin 22 g/dL, hematocrit 68%, MCV 88 fL and ferritin 70 micrograms/L. Hydration is adequate, and there is no headache, visual disturbance or other hyperviscosity symptom. Which approach to the erythrocytosis is best?
options: Start aspirin solely to counter the elevated red-cell mass
Perform isovolumic phlebotomy because hematocrit exceeds 65%
Schedule repeated phlebotomy to achieve the hematocrit target used in polycythemia vera
Maintain hydration and monitor without scheduled phlebotomy
questions.explanation:
Compensated Secondary Erythrocytosis in Cyanotic CHD

Correct answer: Maintain hydration and monitor without scheduled phlebotomy

Adaptive Erythrocytosis

**Higher hemoglobin compensates for reduced saturation and helps maintain oxygen content.**

Hematocrit ==68%== without symptoms or iron deficiency is not a phlebotomy indication.

If Hyperviscosity Symptoms Occur

**Assess hydration and iron indices; correct reversible abnormalities.**

**Exclude alternative causes of headache, dizziness or fatigue.**

Severe headache, fever or focal deficits require urgent assessment for stroke/brain abscess.

**Consider expert isovolumic phlebotomy only for persistent important symptoms, usually Hct ==>65%==, after correction.**

**Monitor saturation, symptoms, CBC and iron stores.**

Repeated venesection can impair oxygen delivery and cause iron deficiency.

Start aspirin solely to counter the elevated red-cell mass: Aspirin has separate vascular indications, but elevated red-cell mass alone does not establish benefit and cyanotic patients may bleed.

Perform isovolumic phlebotomy because hematocrit exceeds 65%: Hct >65% is relevant only with persistent significant hyperviscosity after hydration and iron correction; the supplied patient is asymptomatic.

Schedule repeated phlebotomy to achieve the hematocrit target used in polycythemia vera: Polycythemia vera is clonal with different treatment targets; applying its hematocrit target to hypoxemic adaptation can impair oxygen transport.

questions.question: A cyanotic adult has increasing fatigue, hemoglobin 19 g/dL, hematocrit 60%, MCV 66 fL, ferritin 7 micrograms/L and transferrin saturation 8%. There is no acute bleeding or hemodynamic deterioration. Which strategy best addresses the laboratory abnormality?
options: Replace iron with monitored reassessment of blood count and iron indices
Withhold iron because the hemoglobin is already above the laboratory reference range
Perform venesection before giving iron to prevent a further hematocrit increase
Defer iron until a hemoglobinopathy panel explains the microcytosis
questions.explanation:
Iron Deficiency Despite an Elevated Hemoglobin

Correct answer: Replace iron with monitored reassessment of blood count and iron indices

Iron Deficiency Despite High Hemoglobin

**Ferritin 7 micrograms/L + transferrin saturation ==8%== confirms depleted iron stores.**

Microcytosis supports deficiency; high hemoglobin does not exclude it in chronic hypoxemia.

**Interpret hemoglobin relative to saturation; inflammation can complicate ferritin interpretation.**

Replace and Reassess

**Look for dietary deficiency, menstrual/GI loss and prior phlebotomy.**

**Choose oral or IV iron according to severity and tolerance.**

A small prospective study used ferrous fumarate up to ==200 mg== three times daily for 3 months.

This is iron-salt mass, not elemental iron, and not a mandatory starting regimen.

**Repeat CBC, iron indices and symptoms; assess excessive erythrocytosis or adverse effects.**

Persistent microcytosis after repletion may require a hemoglobinopathy evaluation.

Withhold iron because the hemoglobin is already above the laboratory reference range: Hemoglobin rises adaptively in hypoxemia; low ferritin and transferrin saturation still demonstrate treatable iron deficiency.

Perform venesection before giving iron to prevent a further hematocrit increase: Venesection removes additional iron and red cells. Its narrow hyperviscosity indication does not apply to this iron-deficient presentation.

Defer iron until a hemoglobinopathy panel explains the microcytosis: Thalassemia can coexist, but proven iron depletion already warrants treatment; investigate residual unexplained microcytosis after repletion.

options: BREATHE-5 established bosentan superiority over sildenafil in a direct randomized comparison
MAESTRO met its primary endpoint by improving six-minute walk distance over placebo
BREATHE-5 improved pulmonary vascular resistance without worsening systemic oxygen saturation
MAESTRO demonstrated lower mortality as its primary treatment effect
questions.explanation:
Interpreting Eisenmenger Endothelin-Antagonist Trials

Correct answer: BREATHE-5 improved pulmonary vascular resistance without worsening systemic oxygen saturation

Trial Interpretation

**BREATHE-5: 54 WHO-FC III patients; bosentan versus placebo for 16 weeks.**

PVR improved; systemic saturation safety was preserved; walking distance also improved.

**MAESTRO: 226 patients; macitentan did not meet primary 6-minute-walk superiority.**

Exploratory signals do not convert a negative primary endpoint into proven efficacy or mortality benefit.

Drug Use and Escalation

**Bosentan blocks ETA and ETB: >40-kg adult, ==62.5 mg== twice daily for 4 weeks, then ==125 mg== twice daily.**

LFTs before treatment and monthly; monitor Hb, edema and interactions.

Pregnancy contraindicated; contraception during treatment and for 1 month afterward; hormonal contraceptive efficacy may fall.

**2025: persistent symptoms/worsening exercise on monotherapy with LVEF ==>40%== → ERA + PDE5 inhibitor.**

There have been intermittent minor hemoptysis episodes. Which long-term antithrombotic strategy is most appropriate solely for the Eisenmenger diagnosis?

Do not prescribe routine oral anticoagulation; reassess if a separate indication develops
Start a direct oral anticoagulant because it avoids INR monitoring
Use aspirin as a lower-intensity substitute for preventive anticoagulation
questions.explanation:
Antithrombotic Decisions in Eisenmenger Syndrome

Correct answer: Do not prescribe routine oral anticoagulation; reassess if a separate indication develops

Thrombosis and Bleeding Coexist

**Cyanotic CHD combines stasis/vascular dilation with platelet and coagulation abnormalities.**

Organized in-situ PA thrombus is not automatically equivalent to acute embolism.

**2025: no routine oral anticoagulation solely for Eisenmenger syndrome.**

When an Independent Indication Exists

**Reassess for atrial arrhythmia, proven thromboembolism, mechanical valve or another indication.**

**Review bleeding, platelets, renal/hepatic function and drug interactions.**

Mechanical valves require a vitamin K antagonist, not a DOAC.

**Significant active hemoptysis: urgent assessment, stabilization and selected antithrombotic interruption/reversal.**

**With markedly high hematocrit, ask the laboratory about citrate adjustment for coagulation samples.**

Start a vitamin K antagonist to prevent pulmonary vascular thrombosis: Warfarin may treat an independent indication, but routine Eisenmenger thromboprophylaxis lacks sufficient benefit against the bleeding risk.

Start a direct oral anticoagulant because it avoids INR monitoring: Avoiding INR monitoring is convenient but does not create an indication; a DOAC still requires appropriate risk and organ-function assessment.

Use aspirin as a lower-intensity substitute for preventive anticoagulation: Aspirin treats specific arterial conditions; it is not a proven low-intensity substitute for routine cyanotic-CHD anticoagulation.

questions.question: A 25-year-old with severe tricuspid regurgitation has a septal tricuspid leaflet hinge point 18 mm apical to the anterior mitral leaflet insertion in the four-chamber view. Body surface area is 1.8 m². Which structural diagnosis is best supported?
options: Isolated tricuspid valve dysplasia without Ebstein displacement
Ebstein anomaly
Atrial functional tricuspid regurgitation
Ventricular functional tricuspid regurgitation
questions.explanation:
Indexed Tricuspid Displacement and Ebstein Anatomy

Correct answer: Ebstein anomaly

Diagnostic Anatomy

**Indexed displacement = 18/1.8 = ==10 mm==/m²; ==≥8 mm==/m² supports adult Ebstein anomaly.**

Measure septal tricuspid hinge relative to anterior mitral insertion in the four-chamber view.

**Displaced valve creates atrialized proximal RV and a functional distal RV.**

Assess leaflet morphology, TR and effective RV output; total chamber size can mislead.

Associated Lesions and Intervention

**Look for ASD/PFO-related cyanosis and accessory pathways; CMR quantifies functional RV anatomy.**

**2025: ≥moderate TR with HF, worsening exercise capacity or progressive RV dysfunction → surgery.**

Selected asymptomatic cases: progressive RV enlargement, atrial desaturation, recurrent arrhythmia or paradoxical embolism also support intervention.

**Cone reconstruction preserves native valve tissue when suitable.**

Do not close an atrial outlet without assessing RV filling tolerance.

Isolated tricuspid valve dysplasia without Ebstein displacement: Dysplasia causes malformed leaflets and TR without the characteristic indexed apical displacement demonstrated in this case.

Atrial functional tricuspid regurgitation: Atrial functional TR follows annular/right-atrial dilation; it does not explain congenital displacement of the septal hinge point.

Ventricular functional tricuspid regurgitation: Ventricular functional TR reflects tethering from RV remodeling; the valve attachment itself is not characteristically displaced as supplied.

options: Begin an AV-nodal blocking drug as definitive management of the pre-excitation

Proceed with valve repair and defer pathway assessment until after surgery
Expert electrophysiological study to assess accessory pathways and potential ablation
questions.explanation:
Accessory-Pathway Assessment Before Tricuspid Repair

Correct answer: Expert electrophysiological study to assess accessory pathways and potential ablation

Why Asymptomatic Pre-excitation Matters

**Ebstein anomaly can have multiple or rapidly conducting accessory pathways.**

They support AVRT; pre-excited AF may produce dangerous ventricular rates.

**2025: EP study is recommended for symptomatic arrhythmia or asymptomatic ventricular pre-excitation.**

Coordinate With Tricuspid Surgery

**Map pathway number and conduction risk before surgery when appropriate.**

**Ablate high-risk or multiple pathways using congenital EP expertise.**

Valve repair may make later catheter access more difficult.

**For unstable tachyarrhythmia, use synchronized cardioversion.**

Avoid isolated AV-nodal blockade in irregular pre-excited tachycardia.

**Successful ablation does not treat severe TR; continue structural care.**

Begin an AV-nodal blocking drug as definitive management of the pre-excitation: AV-nodal blockers treat selected regular SVTs but do not eliminate pathways and can be hazardous during pre-excited AF.

Ambulatory monitoring alone, reserving pathway assessment for documented sustained tachycardia: Monitoring can capture episodes but cannot fully assess antegrade conduction risk or exclude multiple pathways in manifest pre-excitation.

Proceed with valve repair and defer pathway assessment until after surgery: Repair can impede later access; absence of palpitations does not remove the rationale for preoperative pathway assessment.

questions.question: A 38-year-old underwent a Senning operation for d-TGA. Resting saturation is 96%, falling reproducibly to 84% on exercise. Systemic RV function is unchanged, with no important new valve regurgitation or pulmonary disease. Which residual lesion should be specifically sought?

Isolated systemic venous baffle stenosis without a leak
Isolated systemic tricuspid regurgitation without a shunt
Isolated chronotropic incompetence from sinus-node dysfunction
questions.explanation:
Exertional Desaturation After an Atrial Switch

Correct answer: A baffle leak allowing systemic venous blood to reach the systemic arterial circuit

Atrial-Switch Circulation

**Mustard/Senning baffles send caval blood to the mitral valve and subpulmonary LV.**

Pulmonary venous blood enters the systemic RV and aorta.

**Baffle leak permits desaturated venous blood into the systemic circuit.**

Exercise-related pressure changes may reveal a leak not obvious at rest.

Investigate and Manage

**Map baffle patency and integrity: contrast echo, CMR and selected TEE/catheterization.**

Arm injection can miss an inferior baffle leak; select the injection site for the anatomy.

**Assess symptomatic leak closure with congenital expertise and hemodynamic review.**

**Before transvenous leads, assess obstruction and systemic embolic risk.**

**Continue surveillance for systemic RV failure, TR, atrial arrhythmia and sinus-node disease.**

Isolated systemic venous baffle stenosis without a leak: Baffle stenosis restricts preload and causes congestion, but without admixture it does not directly explain arterial desaturation.

Isolated systemic tricuspid regurgitation without a shunt: Systemic TR can reduce output but does not create venous-to-arterial mixing; important new regurgitation is also excluded.

Isolated chronotropic incompetence from sinus-node dysfunction: Chronotropic incompetence limits exercise output through heart-rate response, usually without this marked reproducible oxygen-saturation fall.

questions.explanation:
Coronary Assessment After an Arterial Switch

Correct answer: Coronary CT angiography focused on the reimplanted coronary origins and proximal course

Arterial-Switch Complications

**Great arteries are switched and coronaries reimplanted; the LV becomes systemic.**

Late ostial narrowing or proximal kinking can cause ischemia despite young age.

**New exertional symptoms or regional dysfunction warrant coronary evaluation.**

Select the Investigation

**Coronary CTA maps transferred ostia, proximal course and great-vessel relationships.**

**Functional perfusion testing or invasive angiography may clarify significance or persistent unexplained symptoms.**

A normal anatomical study does not exclude every dynamic abnormality.

**This stable case asks anatomy; unstable/ACS presentations need urgent clinical treatment.**

**Long-term follow-up also assesses neoaortic root/valve and neopulmonary/branch PA stenosis.**

Exercise stress echocardiography focused on inducible wall-motion abnormalities: Stress echo detects inducible wall-motion changes but does not usually map the surgically transferred coronary origins.

Vasodilator stress CMR focused on myocardial perfusion: Stress CMR assesses perfusion/ischemia, whereas this question asks directly for reimplanted coronary ostial and proximal anatomy.

Exercise ECG focused on reproducible ST-segment changes: Exercise ECG can link symptoms and ischemic electrical changes; it cannot show ostial narrowing or the proximal coronary course.

questions.question: An adult with an extracardiac Fontan has worsening exercise intolerance despite preserved systemic ventricular ejection fraction and no important AV-valve regurgitation. questions.explanation:

Correct answer: Reduced passive pulmonary flow limits systemic ventricular preload

Passive Pulmonary Flow

**Fontan connects caval return to the pulmonary arteries without a subpulmonary ventricle.**

**Qp depends on (Fontan pressure − pulmonary venous pressure)/PVR.**

Higher PVR reduces flow or requires more upstream venous pressure.

Less pulmonary return → less systemic ventricular preload and stroke volume; EF can remain normal.

Assess the Whole Circuit

**Check pathway/branch PA obstruction, filling pressure, AV-valve disease, rhythm and collaterals.**

**Use catheterization when unexplained deterioration needs pressure/flow assessment.**

**Treat congestion cautiously: excessive diuresis further reduces preload.**

**Selected pulmonary vasodilators may help without elevated ventricular filling pressure.**

They do not correct mechanical pathway obstruction; response is not uniform.

PVR ↑ → Passive pulmonary flow ↓ → Ventricular preload ↓ → Stroke volume ↓ despite preserved EF

Reduced sinus-node responsiveness limits augmentation of cardiac output: Sinus-node dysfunction can impair exercise output, but no abnormal rate response is supplied; increased PVR directly explains reduced preload.

Increased pulmonary resistance directly increases systemic ventricular systolic afterload: Systemic arterial resistance directly determines systemic ejection afterload; pulmonary resistance chiefly limits upstream filling in Fontan physiology.

Reduced ventricular compliance impairs filling at an elevated diastolic pressure: Diastolic stiffness can limit output through high downstream filling pressure, but that pressure is unchanged in this case.

questions.question: A 27-year-old with Fontan circulation develops edema, loose stools and serum albumin 2.1 g/dL. Fecal pancreatic elastase concentration
Quantitative fecal fat excretion
questions.explanation:
Confirming Protein-Losing Enteropathy After Fontan Palliation

Correct answer: Timed fecal alpha-1-antitrypsin clearance with a contemporaneous serum level

Confirm Intestinal Protein Loss

**Timed fecal alpha-1-antitrypsin clearance uses contemporaneous stool and serum measurements.**

Mayo reference ≤27 mL/24 h; diarrhea may raise values and requires qualified interpretation.

GI bleeding can confound results; gastric acid limits assessment of gastric protein loss.

**PLE: low albumin, edema ± diarrhea, immunoglobulin/lymphocyte loss.**

Exclude renal loss, nutrition and hepatic dysfunction; normal INR does not exclude FALD.

Fontan and Lymphatic Management

**Assess pathway obstruction, PVR, ventricular filling, AV-valve disease and rhythm.**

**Support nutrition and fluid balance; correct reversible hemodynamic lesions.**

Albumin provides temporary support, not correction of ongoing leakage.

**Selected patients need lymphatic imaging/intervention or transplant assessment.**

Plastic Bronchitis

**Abnormal pulmonary lymphatic flow causes branching bronchial casts and possible airway obstruction.**

Urgent airway assessment ± bronchoscopic removal; dynamic MR lymphangiography can guide targeted intervention.

Preserved EF does not exclude either lymphatic complication.

Fecal calprotectin concentration: Calprotectin indicates intestinal inflammation and supports IBD assessment; it does not quantify intestinal plasma-protein clearance.

Fecal pancreatic elastase concentration: Elastase evaluates pancreatic insufficiency, with dilutional pitfalls in watery stool; it does not directly demonstrate protein-losing enteropathy.

Quantitative fecal fat excretion: Fecal fat documents fat malabsorption, not plasma-protein leakage; it cannot directly confirm the suspected Fontan complication.

Use anticoagulation only during future documented flutter episodes
questions.explanation:

Fontan Thromboembolic Risk

**Venous stasis, abnormal pathways and sustained atrial arrhythmia add risk beyond CHA2DS2-VASc.**

**A 20-minute documented flutter episode establishes a sustained arrhythmia history.**

Return to sinus rhythm does not remove that history or the Fontan substrate.

Long-Term Strategy

**Initiate oral anticoagulation after agent and bleeding-risk assessment.**

**Review renal/hepatic function, prior bleeding, anatomy, drugs and adherence.**

Do not infer agent equivalence from convenience; comparative Fontan evidence remains limited.

**Lower-risk Fontan adults without high-risk features may receive aspirin or anticoagulation.**

Prior thrombus, embolism, atriopulmonary Fontan or sustained atrial arrhythmia changes the decision.

**Continue rhythm surveillance and evaluate hemodynamic contributors.**

Continue aspirin alone because the conventional stroke score is zero: Aspirin can suit lower-risk Fontan prophylaxis, but sustained flutter is a high-risk feature missed by a conventional zero stroke score.

Withhold antithrombotic therapy unless a second flutter episode occurs: The documented sustained episode already establishes the relevant risk; waiting for recurrence is not required by this pathway.

Use anticoagulation only during future documented flutter episodes: Episode-only treatment ignores persistent Fontan stasis and arrhythmia history; anticoagulation is not limited to detected flutter periods.

questions.question: A 32-year-old, 28 years after Fontan completion, has hepatology-confirmed cirrhosis. Aminotransferases are near normal, ultrasound visualization is adequate and no focal lesion is present. Which surveillance strategy best addresses the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma?

Liver ultrasound at six-month intervals, with AFP as an adjunct
Scheduled repeat liver biopsy to detect early malignant transformation
questions.explanation:
Liver Surveillance in Fontan-Associated Cirrhosis

Correct answer: Liver ultrasound at six-month intervals, with AFP as an adjunct

Cirrhosis and HCC Surveillance

**FALD reflects chronic venous congestion and altered perfusion; quiet liver enzymes do not exclude advanced disease.**

**Confirmed cirrhosis: surveillance at least every 6 months.**

EASL-ERN: experienced ultrasound with AFP adjunct; normal AFP does not exclude HCC.

Poor visualization or suspicious nodules require appropriate multiphase CT/MRI.

Interpret Results in Fontan Context

**Elastography reflects congestion plus fibrosis; ordinary fibrosis cutoffs may misclassify FALD.**

**Assess platelets, spleen, varices, ascites and serial imaging.**

Regenerative nodules can be benign; indeterminate lesions may need targeted biopsy.

**Coordinate hepatology and ACHD care; review circuit pressures and transplant implications.**

Routine repeat biopsy is not a substitute for tumor surveillance.

Annual elastography, with imaging for a focal lesion only if stiffness increases: Elastography can contribute longitudinal information, but stiffness is affected by venous congestion and does not screen directly for focal malignancy. A stable stiffness value does not replace scheduled tumor surveillance.

Annual aminotransferases, with liver imaging when enzymes rise: Annual laboratory assessment is part of Fontan organ surveillance, but aminotransferases may remain near normal despite advanced disease. Waiting for enzyme elevation can miss an asymptomatic hepatic tumor.

Scheduled repeat liver biopsy to detect early malignant transformation: Biopsy is useful for selected diagnostic or transplant-related questions and indeterminate lesions. Repeated nontargeted biopsy is not the routine method for detecting new focal HCC and exposes the patient to procedural risk and sampling limitations.

questions.explanation:
New Atrial Flutter and Fontan Hemodynamic Deterioration

Correct answer: Plan timely rhythm restoration with thrombus assessment and anticoagulation, while evaluating the Fontan circuit

Why Flutter Destabilizes Fontan Flow

**Loss of effective atrial rhythm impairs filling even after the ventricular rate slows.**

AV-valve disease, relaxation abnormalities and pulmonary venous flow changes may amplify the effect.

Restore Rhythm and Assess the Circuit

**2025: timely cardioversion for new atrial flutter/AF.**

Stable patients need thrombus assessment, anticoagulation and selected imaging; short reported duration does not eliminate risk.

**Instability: urgent synchronized cardioversion; do not wait for an elective anticoagulation interval.**

**Plan sedation/ventilation to preserve preload and low PVR.**

Avoid excessive airway pressure, hypoxemia and acidosis.

**Search for obstruction/thrombosis, AV-valve disease and ventricular/filling abnormalities.**

Consider congenital EP ablation, recurrence monitoring and advanced Fontan assessment if deterioration persists.

Start pulmonary vasodilator treatment and reserve cardioversion for failure of that therapy: Vasodilators help selected pulmonary vascular limitation; they do not replace treatment of new flutter and require filling-pressure assessment.

Continue rate control alone and reassess ventricular function at routine follow-up: Rate slowing can stabilize initially, but persistent Fontan symptoms require timely rhythm restoration and evaluation rather than routine delayed review.

Escalate diuresis first and defer rhythm restoration until congestion has resolved: Diuresis helps congestion but can reduce preload; the arrhythmia itself needs treatment instead of waiting for full decongestion.

Why Flutter Destabilizes Fontan Flow

  • Loss of effective atrial rhythm impairs filling even after the ventricular rate slows.
    • AV-valve disease, relaxation abnormalities and pulmonary venous flow changes may amplify the effect.

Restore Rhythm and Assess the Circuit

  1. 2025: timely cardioversion for new atrial flutter/AF.
    • Stable patients need thrombus assessment, anticoagulation and selected imaging; short reported duration does not eliminate risk.
  2. Instability: urgent synchronized cardioversion; do not wait for an elective anticoagulation interval.
  3. Plan sedation/ventilation to preserve preload and low PVR.
    • Avoid excessive airway pressure, hypoxemia and acidosis.
  4. Search for obstruction/thrombosis, AV-valve disease and ventricular/filling abnormalities.
    • Consider congenital EP ablation, recurrence monitoring and advanced Fontan assessment if deterioration persists.

Other Options

  • A — Start pulmonary vasodilator treatment and reserve cardioversion for failure of that therapy: Vasodilators help selected pulmonary vascular limitation; they do not replace treatment of new flutter and require filling-pressure assessment.
  • B — Continue rate control alone and reassess ventricular function at routine follow-up: Rate slowing can stabilize initially, but persistent Fontan symptoms require timely rhythm restoration and evaluation rather than routine delayed review.
  • C — Escalate diuresis first and defer rhythm restoration until congestion has resolved: Diuresis helps congestion but can reduce preload; the arrhythmia itself needs treatment instead of waiting for full decongestion.
