questions.question: CMR in an asymptomatic adult shows one right upper pulmonary vein draining to the SVC, an intact atrial septum, Qp/Qs 1.2 and a mildly enlarged RV with normal function. Pulmonary pressure is normal and serial measurements are stable. Which strategy is best supported?
options: Continue congenital cardiology surveillance without repair at present
Refer for surgical redirection based on the anomalous connection alone
Plan covered-stent correction using the sinus venosus ASD pathway
Perform invasive hemodynamic assessment before deciding whether any observation is acceptable
questions.explanation:
Small Isolated Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Shunt

Correct answer: Continue congenital cardiology surveillance without repair at present

Isolated Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Drainage

**Oxygenated pulmonary venous blood enters systemic veins, recirculating through RA/RV despite an intact atrial septum.**

Shunt burden depends on the number, size and lung territory of anomalous veins.

**2025: Qp/Qs <1.5 with normal/mildly enlarged RV → no surgical repair indication.**

Surveillance and Related Anatomy

**Track symptoms, RV size/function and pulmonary pressures; CMR quantifies flow and maps veins.**

CT is an anatomical alternative; deterioration or significant volume loading prompts repair reassessment.

**Scimitar: right pulmonary vein usually drains to IVC.**

Curved right-border vein may accompany right-lung hypoplasia and abnormal systemic arterial supply.

**Repair can cause pulmonary/systemic venous obstruction or rhythm complications; establish benefit first.**

Refer for surgical redirection based on the anomalous connection alone: Surgical redirection treats significant attributable loading, not every anatomical anomaly; this small stable shunt has no demonstrated repair benefit.

Plan covered-stent correction using the sinus venosus ASD pathway: Covered-stent correction applies to selected sinus venosus anatomy; an isolated anomalous vein with intact septum is a different target.

Perform invasive hemodynamic assessment before deciding whether any observation is acceptable: Catheterization resolves suspected PAH or discordant hemodynamics. Clear stable CMR findings do not require invasion merely to justify observation.

Congenital valvar mitral stenosis
Pulmonary vein stenosis
questions.explanation:
Localizing Obstruction in Cor Triatriatum Sinister

Correct answer: Cor triatriatum sinister

Appendage Landmark

**Cor triatriatum: proximal chamber receives pulmonary veins; distal chamber contains LAA and mitral valve.**

Small membrane openings obstruct pulmonary venous return and mimic mitral stenosis.

**Supramitral ring usually lies below the LAA, close to the valve.**

Assess and Treat

**Echo/TEE: define membrane openings, gradient and valve anatomy.**

CT/CMR maps associated pulmonary veins and congenital lesions.

**Interpret gradients with flow, heart rate and symptoms; catheterize selected uncertain cases.**

**Attributable symptomatic obstruction → surgical membrane resection.**

Severe asymptomatic obstruction merits expert assessment; nonobstructive incidental membranes may be observed.

**Diuretics relieve congestion temporarily; follow residual obstruction, pulmonary veins and rhythm.**

Supramitral ring: A supramitral ring usually lies below the appendage; here the appendage is downstream with the mitral valve.

Congenital valvar mitral stenosis: Valvar stenosis involves the mitral apparatus; the supplied normally opening valve and separate membrane localize obstruction elsewhere.

Pulmonary vein stenosis: Pulmonary vein stenosis obstructs venous entry, not a membrane dividing pulmonary venous and appendage-containing atrial chambers.

questions.question: A 24-year-old has exertional chest pain and presyncope. Coronary CT shows the left coronary artery arising from the right sinus with a slit-like ostium and proximal intramural segment. Stress imaging demonstrates ischemia in its territory, without atherosclerotic disease. Which management strategy is most appropriate?
options: Proceed directly to coronary stenting as for an atherosclerotic ostial lesion
Use antianginal medication with imaging surveillance as the definitive strategy
Refer for congenital coronary surgical repair assessment
Implant a prophylactic ICD before addressing the coronary anomaly
questions.explanation:
Ischemic Anomalous Aortic Coronary Origin

Correct answer: Refer for congenital coronary surgical repair assessment

High-Risk Coronary Phenotype

**Opposite-sinus left coronary origin + slit-like ostium/intramural course + attributable ischemia warrants surgical assessment.**

CT defines origin/course; stress imaging tests functional consequence.

**A negative stress test does not automatically neutralize high-risk anatomy in another patient.**

Repair and Follow-Up

**Select unroofing, reimplantation or another reconstruction from actual anatomy.**

Consider aortic commissural relationships and valve-injury risk.

**Restrict strenuous exertion pending assessment of this symptomatic ischemic presentation.**

**Assess ventricular function, scar and arrhythmias; reassess before return to sport.**

Follow patency, residual ischemia and AR; repair is not a guarantee against every event.

**Asymptomatic or benign-course variants require separate assessment.**

Proceed directly to coronary stenting as for an atherosclerotic ostial lesion: PCI treats acquired stenosis and selected anomalies; this intramural congenital origin needs anatomical surgical consideration, not automatic plaque-style stenting.

Use antianginal medication with imaging surveillance as the definitive strategy: Medication/surveillance can suit selected lower-risk or inoperable patients; attributable ischemia with this anatomy supports surgical correction.

Implant a prophylactic ICD before addressing the coronary anomaly: An ICD treats established arrhythmic risk but does not relieve coronary compromise; this history does not supply a device indication instead of repair.

questions.question: An asymptomatic 30-year-old is found to have the left coronary artery originating from the pulmonary artery. There are extensive right-to-left coronary collaterals and retrograde flow into the pulmonary artery. LV ejection fraction is 58%. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Use a negative stress study as the criterion for avoiding repair
Observe until LV ejection fraction falls because collateral supply is currently adequate
Refer for surgical restoration of a two-coronary system
Close the pulmonary origin alone and retain collateral-dependent single-coronary supply
questions.explanation:
Adult ALCAPA and Restoration of Coronary Supply

Correct answer: Refer for surgical restoration of a two-coronary system

Why Collaterals Do Not Establish Safety

**ALCAPA: left coronary arises from PA; RCA collaterals permit adult survival.**

Retrograde runoff into low-pressure PA creates steal; preserved resting EF does not eliminate ischemic/SCD risk.

**Manifestations include LV dysfunction, arrhythmia and ischemic/functional MR.**

Restore a Two-Coronary Circulation

**Map coronary anatomy and collaterals with cross-sectional imaging; assess LV, MR and scar.**

**Current guidance recommends surgical repair, including asymptomatic adults.**

Reimplantation when feasible or another anatomical reconstruction supplies the left coronary territory.

**Negative stress testing is not a criterion for avoiding recommended repair.**

**Follow patency, ventricular recovery, MR and arrhythmias.**

Existing scar may persist after perfusion is restored.

Use a negative stress study as the criterion for avoiding repair: Stress studies assess functional consequences but cannot guarantee long-term safety; surgery is not conditional on a positive test.

Observe until LV ejection fraction falls because collateral supply is currently adequate: Collaterals explain survival but do not abolish ischemia/SCD risk; waiting for falling EF delays the recommended anatomical repair.

Close the pulmonary origin alone and retain collateral-dependent single-coronary supply: Ligation alone removes runoff but leaves collateral-dependent supply; the usual objective is a reliable two-coronary system.

questions.question: A 26-year-old with Eisenmenger syndrome from a large VSD is considering pregnancy. She is in functional class II on PAH treatment and has preserved LV ejection fraction. Which 2025 ESC mWHO 2.0 maternal cardiovascular risk class applies?
options: Class III
Class II
Class II–III
Class IV
questions.explanation:
Pregnancy Counseling in Eisenmenger Syndrome

Correct answer: Class IV

Pregnancy Risk Is Not Symptom Class

**Eisenmenger/PAH → mWHO 2.0 class IV, despite functional class II or preserved LVEF.**

Pregnancy can worsen right-to-left shunting, RV failure, hypoxemia and embolic risk.

Delivery and postpartum remain hazardous even after an uneventful early pregnancy.

Counseling and Management

**Pregnancy Heart Team: explain maternal/fetal risks, advise avoidance and discuss reliable contraception.**

**Avoid estrogen-containing contraception in cyanotic CHD; individualize long-acting methods and insertion setting.**

**Review PAH drugs: ERAs carry fetal risk; bosentan may reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy.**

Do not abruptly stop essential therapy without specialist planning.

**If pregnant: prompt shared discussion of all options, including termination.**

If continuing, coordinate maternal-fetal, ACHD, PH and anesthesia care through postpartum.

Class III: Class III is high risk, but Eisenmenger belongs in the exceptionally high-risk class IV despite improved functional status.

Class II: Class II represents substantially lower risk. Mild symptoms and preserved LV function do not remove Eisenmenger pulmonary vascular hazards.

Class II–III: II–III is an intermediate category, not an average of reassuring LV function and severe pulmonary vascular disease.

questions.question: Four adults are scheduled for dental extraction involving gingival manipulation. None has previous endocarditis or a prosthetic valve. Under AHA prevention guidance, which congenital finding supports antibiotic prophylaxis?
options: A residual VSD jet adjacent to a prosthetic patch placed five years ago
A completely closed secundum ASD device placed five years ago with no residual defect
An isolated bicuspid aortic valve with mild regurgitation
A small unrepaired acyanotic muscular VSD without prior endocarditis
questions.explanation:
Dental Prophylaxis After Congenital Defect Repair

Correct answer: A residual VSD jet adjacent to a prosthetic patch placed five years ago

Who Needs Dental Prophylaxis?

**Residual shunt adjacent to prosthetic patch/device qualifies, including years after repair.**

**Other high-risk groups: prior IE, prosthetic valves/repair material, unrepaired cyanotic CHD and transplant structural valvular disease.**

**Relevant procedure: gingival manipulation, periapical work or mucosal perforation.**

Adult Regimen and Prevention

**Amoxicillin ==2 g== orally once, 30–60 minutes before the procedure.**

Prophylaxis is not a multi-day course or treatment for established IE.

**Check allergy: clindamycin is no longer recommended by AHA.**

Avoid cephalosporins after penicillin-associated anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.

**Maintain oral hygiene and regular dental care; evaluate unexplained fever.**

Suspected IE requires cultures and treatment assessment; document the actual prophylaxis indication.

A completely closed secundum ASD device placed five years ago with no residual defect: A remote completely closed ASD without residual defect lacks this continuing high-risk anatomical indication; adjacent residual flow changes eligibility.

An isolated bicuspid aortic valve with mild regurgitation: Native bicuspid valve disease increases IE risk but alone is not an AHA highest-risk indication for dental prophylaxis.

A small unrepaired acyanotic muscular VSD without prior endocarditis: An unrepaired acyanotic muscular VSD alone does not qualify; unrepaired cyanotic disease and adjacent prosthetic residual defects are different categories.

questions.question: A stable adult with repaired congenital heart disease reports no limitation but has gradually stopped climbing stairs and cycling. Resting echocardiography is unchanged. The patient can exercise and has no acute illness or test contraindication. Which investigation best quantifies integrated exercise capacity and guides individualized activity advice?
options: Six-minute walk testing with distance and oxygen saturation measurement
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing with gas exchange, ECG and oxygen saturation monitoring
Ambulatory ECG monitoring during usual daily activity
Cardiac magnetic resonance measurement of ventricular volumes and flows
questions.explanation:
Objective Functional Assessment Before Exercise Advice

Correct answer: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing with gas exchange, ECG and oxygen saturation monitoring

Why CPET?

**Patients may reduce activity and report no symptoms despite deteriorating capacity.**

**CPET integrates cardiac delivery, ventilation, gas exchange, conditioning and effort.**

Interpret and Prescribe Activity

**Review peak VO2, ventilatory efficiency, heart-rate/BP response, saturation and rhythm.**

**Interpret low peak VO2 with effort and conditioning; assess chronotropic limitation and exercise desaturation.**

**Compare serial tests using similar protocols and clinical conditions.**

**Tailor exercise to ventricular function, PA pressure, aorta, rhythm risk and cyanosis.**

Encourage appropriate activity; severe obstruction, aortopathy or uncontrolled arrhythmia changes intensity/supervision.

Use alternatives such as 6-minute walk when CPET is unsafe or unreliable.

Six-minute walk testing with distance and oxygen saturation measurement: Six-minute walk is useful in PAH or when CPET is impractical, but provides less complete gas-exchange and ventilatory assessment.

Ambulatory ECG monitoring during usual daily activity: Ambulatory ECG detects intermittent rhythm problems but does not quantify standardized oxygen uptake or integrated exercise capacity.

Cardiac magnetic resonance measurement of ventricular volumes and flows: CMR defines resting anatomy, volumes and flows; it cannot replace graded assessment of exertional physiology and rhythm.

questions.question: A clinically stable 31-year-old with Fontan circulation is scheduled for elective laparoscopic abdominal surgery. Ventricular ejection fraction is preserved, but there is mild cyanosis and Fontan-associated liver disease. Which preoperative approach is most appropriate?
options: Obtain CPET and base the perioperative support plan on peak oxygen consumption
Calculate the Revised Cardiac Risk Index and use it to select the postoperative care setting
Arrange ACHD and anesthesia planning of physiology, procedure location and postoperative support
Arrange diagnostic Fontan catheterization before deciding the operative location
questions.explanation:
Planning Noncardiac Surgery in Fontan Circulation

Correct answer: Arrange ACHD and anesthesia planning of physiology, procedure location and postoperative support

Preoperative ACHD Assessment

**Combine anatomy, current physiology, organ disease and procedural stress; preserved EF alone is insufficient.**

**Review rhythm, oxygenation, venous pathways, ventricular/AV-valve function, liver/renal status and antithrombotics.**

**ACHD/anesthesia team selects location, investigations, optimization and postoperative resources.**

Fontan Anesthesia Priorities

**Protect venous return and low PVR during ventilation, pneumoperitoneum and positioning.**

**Avoid hypoxemia, hypercapnia, acidosis and marked hypovolemia.**

Balance fluid against congestion; neither unrestricted loading nor aggressive depletion is appropriate.

**Use meticulous air precautions when right-to-left pathways exist; plan unusual venous access.**

**Plan pain control, rhythm monitoring, fluid shifts and individualized anticoagulant interruption/resumption.**

Monitoring intensity depends on risk, not a universal ICU rule.

Obtain CPET and base the perioperative support plan on peak oxygen consumption: CPET measures reserve but cannot independently plan for pneumoperitoneum, ventilation or hepatic bleeding risks; multidisciplinary integration is required.

Calculate the Revised Cardiac Risk Index and use it to select the postoperative care setting: RCRI adds acquired-disease risk information but does not adequately encode Fontan pathways, cyanosis or venous-pressure-related organ complications.

Arrange diagnostic Fontan catheterization before deciding the operative location: Catheterization addresses specific pressure/obstruction questions, not a mandatory test for every stable Fontan patient before surgery.

questions.question: A 23-year-old with repaired TOF feels well and asks to stop cardiology follow-up. Current assessment shows normal ventricular function, mild pulmonary regurgitation and no significant residual obstruction. Which follow-up strategy is best supported?
options: Arrange annual ACHD visits with annual CMR irrespective of serial findings
Schedule the next ACHD visit in five years with earlier review for symptoms
Arrange annual general cardiology review and obtain CMR only if symptoms appear
Continue periodic ACHD review with testing intervals tailored to current physiology
questions.explanation:
Lifelong Surveillance After Tetralogy Repair

Correct answer: Continue periodic ACHD review with testing intervals tailored to current physiology

Why Lifelong Review?

**TOF repair leaves risks of pulmonary valve dysfunction, residual obstruction, RV remodeling and scar arrhythmia.**

Self-limited activity can conceal deterioration; symptoms alone are insufficient surveillance.

Routine and Triggered Follow-Up

**2025 physiological stages A/B: ACHD visits every 12–24 months.**

**Normal ventricular function and no more than mild PR: CMR every 3–5 years.**

Do not confuse imaging intervals with clinical visit intervals.

**Earlier review for palpitations, syncope, desaturation, exercise decline or changing imaging.**

Select rhythm monitoring, CPET and imaging according to the concern.

**Address exercise, reproductive health, procedures and acquired risk; preserve repair records.**

Intervals are lesion-specific and become closer with physiological deterioration.

Arrange annual ACHD visits with annual CMR irrespective of serial findings: Annual CMR can suit significant residual disease, but stable normal-function/mild-PR physiology does not justify that intensity automatically.

Schedule the next ACHD visit in five years with earlier review for symptoms: A five-year CMR interval may fit stable TOF, but it should not replace the recommended 12–24-month clinical review.

Arrange annual general cardiology review and obtain CMR only if symptoms appear: Shared cardiology care helps access, but symptom-only CMR may miss RV remodeling; planned congenital and objective surveillance remains needed.

ACC/AHA multisociety ACHD guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.09.006
